newsitem.title: USA: Clinton promises exhaustive probe of Gulf War ills.
newsitem.headline: Clinton promises exhaustive probe of Gulf War ills.

text.p: President Clinton, honouring U.S. veterans Monday, pledged to find the causes of sickness among many who served in the Gulf War and praised the war hero he bested in the battle for the White House, Bob Dole.

Leading the nation in paying tribute to the sacrifices of U.S. armed forces, Clinton reassured Gulf War veterans that his administration was making every effort to learn why many of them had developed unexplained illnesses.

He also used his Veterans' Day address at Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington to try to bind up the wounds of his political conflict with Dole and to highlight parts of his second-term foreign-policy agenda.

"I want to assure all of you that we will leave no stone unturned in our efforts to investigate these cases and to provide our Gulf War veterans with the medical care they need," he told a large crowd huddled on a blustery, cold day in the outdoor amphitheater at the Tomb of the Unknowns.
He said the presidential advisory commission he had appointed to respond to the health concerns of Gulf veterans would hand in its report by the end of the year.

"There are mysteries still unanswered and we must do more, but the United States will not forget the people who have served us and we will discharge our obligation to those who served in the Persian Gulf," Clinton said as the veterans and their families broke into loud applause.

The Pentagon denies it covered up troops' possible exposure to chemical weapons in the 1991 Gulf conflict, saying there was no evidence of U.S. deaths or injuries from chemical agents or of Iraqi use of them against U.S. forces.

But the Pentagon said on Oct. 20 it was notifying about 20,000 U.S. Gulf War veterans they might have been exposed to chemical weapons after U.S. forces destroyed the Kamisiyah weapons dump in March 1991.

The Washington Post said last week that the presidential panel's preliminary report had found no evidence that chemical weapons had caused the illnesses of Gulf veterans. But the report also said a final decision would have to wait until more than 100 studies by government and civilian researchers were completed, according to the Post.

After laying a wreath at Arlington, Clinton opened his remarks with a tribute to Dole, recalling that the former Republican senator and presidential candidate had nearly been killed by a German shell in World War II.

"He would bear the burden of his severe injury from that day forward for the rest of his life. But he refused to withdraw from the world and instead dedicated his life to serving the American people," Clinton said. "I ask all of you now to join me in applauding his remarkable record of achievement and patriotism for America."

A generation younger than Dole, Clinton avoided service in the Vietnam War and has presided over a considerable reduction in the size of the military since taking office in 1993. But he said America must remain the world's strongest force for peace and freedom.
In an apparent reference to U.S. peacekeeping forces in Bosnia, he said America must continue to confront the violent ethnic conflicts "that so bedevil the world today."

"We must strengthen and expand the alliances that have brought us thus far," Clinton added, apparently referring to the NATO alliance, which his administration wants to expand to include several Central European nations by 1999.

Clinton said the 1.5 million U.S. men and women in uniform must have the best equipment and training and Washington must help veterans with their education, jobs, homes and health. One media report last week said about a third of the men who went to homeless shelters in the past year were veterans.

The president did not refer to a widening sex scandal at an Army training base in Maryland where about 20 supervisors have been suspended pending an investigation and three Army trainers face charges for allegedly sexually harassing young female recruits and coercing them into having sex.
